name: Muyuw
confidence_why: Lithgow and Lithgow 1974 mark stress on every dictionary entry and give minimal pairs (túwan/tuwán, imóm/ímoum) without stating a rule, but their 1973 verb manuscript calls stress predictable on the penultimate syllable in the overwhelming majority of words, with final stress only where a stem-final vowel drops before the zero third-singular object suffix, and Lithgow 1978 marks the penult on every polysyllabic noun, so the evidence, all from one family's fieldwork, favours penultimate stress with morphological exceptions over a lexical system.

catalog_quote: It is essential to stress the right vowel in a word. For instance túwan "his older brother" tuwán "his older brothers" imóm "he drank it" (transitive) ímoum "he is drinking" (intransitive) Stress is indicated in this dictionary, but we do not write it in Muyuw books. ... Unstressed vowels are frequently dropped, especially from long words. ... Unstressed vowels in the early syllables of long words may be dropped completely or partially.

new_statements.quote: They are made in a regular pattern of sound with certain syllables stressed or lengthened, and others short or unstressed. In Muyuw the last vowel of most words is lengthened, and most words end in a consonant. [...] The words for 'father' illustrate this: Muyuw tʌ́ma.n / Dobu tʌ́ma.nʌ. In each case the vowel before the last consonant is lengthened, and this is a good help in deciding where a word ends. However some suffixes on the end of Muyuw words make patterns which differ from the basic word-pattern. [p. 21:] Muyuw words pattern differently when the stress or accent is on different syllables.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened; PDF page 15 (printed p. 31, section 12 'Words') rendered and read against the image: every sentence of the quotation is there word for word, and the p. 21 sentence ('Muyuw words pattern differently when the stress or accent is on different syllables') is on PDF page 5, section 4. The example is printed 'Muyuw tʌ́ma.n / Dobu tʌ́ma.nʌ' with the acute on the first (penultimate) vowel and the length dot after the final vowel, as the compiler says. Where I disagree is the classification. the compiler took the prose statement 'the last vowel of most words is lengthened' as the stress statement and coded fixed: final syllable, while treating the acute as unexplained. But section 4 def…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Muyuw has an empty rule field, so this is the first placement statement held by the project: surface prominence (lengthening) on the last vowel of most, consonant-final, words. It is compatible with the penultimate stress rule in the project's other held Muyuw source (Lithgow & Lithgow 1973, 'Muyuw verbs', see reasoning), because that rule counts an underlying stem-final vowel that is elided word-finally.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level prominence is described as lengthening: in most Muyuw words, which end in a consonant, the last vowel (the vowel before the final consonant) is lengthened, i.e. surface prominence on the final syllable; the paper does not separate stress from length ('stressed or lengthened'). In the printed example tʌ́ma.n 'father' the length mark sits on the final vowel while an acute sits on the initial vowel (the same marking is given for Dobu tʌ́ma.nʌ), so the acute may mark something other than the lengthening peak; the paper does not explain it.
new_statements.exceptions: Some suffixes change the basic word pattern (the -emi suffix of Section 8); with the compound-final -wan 'actually' the vowel before -wan stays lengthened and -wan itself is not lengthened; stress/accent position differs between word classes and with affixation (p. 21).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Muyuw of Woodlark Island (Lithgow 1978, p. 18: 'the Muyuw language of Woodlark Island'); no dialect is named. Lithgow 1978 also contains Dobu and Duna examples, which were excluded.

new_statements.citation: Lithgow, David (1969). Muyuw clause types and structure. 29 pp.
new_statements.check: reported on verification, not yet confirmed
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Work 1 (Lithgow 1969, Muyuw clause types and structure), p. 22 of the manuscript (PDF page 25), section 5.9.4 Post-positional Modifiers: 'these modifiers follow the word which they modify, and carry a lighter stress' - a phrase-level prominence remark about modifiers such as -wan 'actually', not a word-stress rule; it matches Lithgow 1978 p. 31 where the vowel of -wan is said not to be lengthened. Work 0 (Lithgow, Daphne 1970, The discourse in Muyuw) says nothing about stress. there was appended with both entries and the re-check of.

readall_conflicts: No genuine disagreement, but two levels of description. Lithgow 1978 (p. 31) states that the last vowel of most Muyuw words is lengthened and most words end in a consonant (surface prominence on the final syllable), while the project's held manuscript Lithgow & Lithgow 1973 'Muyuw verbs' (pp. 6-8, 18, not in the target list) states that stress is 'predictable (penultimate syllable) in an overwhelming majority of words' and that verb stems are CVCV underlyingly with the final vowel elided word-finally (CVCV -> CVC), so that the stressed stem vowel ends up in the final surface syllable when the 3sg object suffix is zero (i-gút-ø 'he pulls it out', ʌ-bɛ́s-ø 'I pierce it', b-i-ván-ø 'he will stand on it') but in the penult when nothing is elided (í-gut 'he pulls out', i-gútu-gw 'he pulls me out', á-bas 'I am piercing', b-é-van, b-é-van-s). The 1978 lengthened 'last vowel' is that same vowel. The one unexplained detail is the acute on the initial vowel of tʌ́ma.n in the 1978 paper alongside the length mark on the final vowel.

audit.recode_to: PENULTIMATE default (right-edge, weight-insensitive) with morphologically conditioned final stress (transitive verbs with zero 3sg object, where the final stem vowel is elided and stress stays on the old penult; non-inclusive plural of inalienably possessed kin nouns, e.g. túwan/tuwán; monosyllabic transitive stems ibɛ́s vs prefix-stressed intransitives ímad) - i.e. positional-penult + morphological, not lexical. Cite Lithgow & Lithgow 1973 ms pp. 6-8 and Lithgow 1978 pp. 21-24, 31 alongside the 1974 dictionary pp. 8-11, 17; strength of the evidence page-image for all.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on printed p. 8 (image viewed) with the remainder on p. 9 (two scanned layers); locator and citation are correct. (2) The deciding source is a 1974 SIL dictionary front-matter that marks stress per entry but states no rule; lexical was an inference from silence, and the compilers already flagged set by morphology as defensible. (3) The same authors' descriptive papers, downloaded now from the SIL archive via the Internet Archive, do address position: the 1973 'Muyuw verbs' ms has a 'Stress rule' section saying stress is penultimate and 'predictable (penultimate syllable) in an overwhelming majority of words', with surface-final stress in transitive 3sg-object forms explained by final-vowel elision; Lithgow 1978 (published, WPNGL 25) marks stress on the penult in every polysyllabic 'common pattern' noun it lists and shows the prefix-vs-stem alte

sources.quote: p.6: 'Pure intransitive verb stems ... í-gig "he laughs", í-kʌlivʌ́tɔw "he falls". Note that in these verbs the stress falls on the penultimate syllable.
